« Briquet » désignait autrefois un chien: “Briquet” once meant a medium-sized scent hound, and this is the only breed to have kept the name. Bred before World War I by the Comte d'Elva as a well-proportioned, scaled-down Grand Griffon Vendéen, the Briquet type was nearly wiped out by wars several times before reappearing in Fontenay-le-Comte in 1946. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 19), it shares its club with the three other Vendéen griffons, and its packs shine in field trials, as shown by a Coupe de France on roe deer won in 1995. Its numbers remain modest but are growing (174 dogs registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025).

Ancien chien d'eau français remontant au: An old French water dog dating back to the 16th century, used for centuries to locate, flush and retrieve waterfowl in marshes and rivers. The breed's name comes from “barbe” (French for beard). Almost extinct after World War II, it was saved by devoted breeders.
Ancien chien de ferme polyvalent de la p: An old all-purpose farm dog from the Iberian Peninsula, used for centuries in Spain to herd livestock, retrieve waterfowl for hunters and help fishermen. Nearly extinct, it was successfully restored by dedicated breeders.
Ancien lévrier à la silhouette haute, él: An ancient sighthound with a tall, slender, elegant build designed for exceptional speed. Known for its gentle temperament and often described as a “70 km/h couch potato”, it combines incredible athleticism with calm at home.
Ancienne race allemande (Zwergpinscher): An old German breed (Zwergpinscher) developed centuries ago to hunt rats in houses and stables. It is not a miniaturized Doberman but a separate, older breed, probably descended from the German Pinscher with some Dachshund and Italian Greyhound blood.
Ancienne race allemande développée pour: An old German breed developed for pest control, ratting and farm work. Ancestor of the Doberman Pinscher and the Miniature Pinscher. It nearly disappeared after World War II but was revived by Werner Jung.
Ancienne race de berger écossaise dévelo: An old Scottish herding breed developed to drive sheep and cattle in the harsh conditions of the Highlands, bred for its hardiness, intelligence and ability to work on its own. Almost extinct after World War II, it was saved by devoted breeders.
Ancienne race de berger française dévelo: An old French herding breed, developed over centuries to guard and protect flocks. It served the French army in World War I as a sentry, messenger and pack animal. Nearly extinct after the two world wars, it was saved by devoted enthusiasts.
Ancienne race de berger française, aussi: An old French herding breed, also called the Berger de Beauce, developed on the plains of the Paris Basin to drive and protect flocks of sheep. A cousin of the Briard, from which it was separated in the late 19th century, it served as a messenger and guard dog in both World Wars.
Ancienne race de berger hongroise amenée: An ancient Hungarian herding breed brought by the Magyar tribes more than 1,000 years ago, traditionally used to herd and guard flocks on the Hungarian plains. Its unique corded coat protected it from bad weather and predators.
Ancienne race de bouvier du Pembrokeshir: An old cattle-herding breed from Pembrokeshire, in Wales. According to tradition, its ancestors arrived with Flemish weavers in 1107. Its small size let it nip at the cattle's heels while dodging their kicks.
Ancienne race de garde de troupeaux orig: An ancient livestock guardian breed from the Kangal district in Sivas province, Turkey. Used for centuries by shepherds to protect flocks against wolves, bears and jackals, it is considered a Turkish national treasure.
Ancienne race de gardien développée dans: An ancient guardian breed developed in the Himalayas, used by Tibetan nomads and monasteries to protect livestock, villages and camps. It was long presented as the ancestor of modern molossers, a theory that is now debated.
Ancienne race de spitz du peuple sami, e: An ancient spitz breed of the Sami people of Lapland, used to gather, drive and protect reindeer herds. Nearly gone after World War II, it was successfully restored by Finnish breeders.
Ancienne race du Mexique, qui existe en: An ancient breed from Mexico that comes in three sizes (standard, intermediate and miniature) and two varieties, hairless or short-coated. It is known for its loyal, calm and alert temperament.
Ancienne race finlandaise développée au: An ancient Finnish breed developed over the centuries through selection for hunting all kinds of game, from squirrels to bears. It was nearly extinct by the late 19th century, before restoration efforts began, and went on to become the national dog of Finland.
Ancienne race galloise sélectionnée pour: An old Welsh breed developed to flush and retrieve game birds; spaniels are already mentioned in Welsh laws from the 10th century. The British Kennel Club recognized it as a separate breed in 1902.
Ancienne race hollandaise développée dès: An old Dutch breed developed as early as the 16th century to work as a duck decoy dog, luring ducks into traps called “eendenkooien”. Nearly extinct after World War II, it was saved and re-established by Baroness van Hardenbroek.
Ancienne race hongroise d'origine asiati: An ancient Hungarian breed of Asian origin that arrived in the Carpathian Basin with the Magyar tribes. A formidable livestock guardian, it was also the guard dog of the kings and nobility of Hungary, prized for its loyalty and courage.
Ancienne race irlandaise utilisée depuis: An old Irish breed used for more than 200 years as a versatile farm dog for herding livestock, guarding the farm and hunting vermin. Nicknamed “the poor man's wolfhound”, because peasants, who were not allowed to own the hunting dogs of the nobility, used it for everything. Recognized by the Irish Kennel Club in 1937.
Ancienne race italienne descendant des c: An ancient Italian breed descended from Roman molosser war dogs, developed as a versatile farm dog, guardian and big-game hunter. The breed came close to extinction but was revived by enthusiasts in the 1970s and 1980s.
Ancienne race italienne, notamment piémo: An old Italian breed, from Piedmont in particular, that some authors trace back to antiquity without solid evidence. It is in any case depicted from the Renaissance onward, and was bred as a versatile pointing dog for hunting in dense, thorny cover, in woodland as well as in marshes.
Ancienne race japonaise de type spitz à: An ancient Japanese spitz-type breed with a small, compact, well-muscled build and a distinctive fox-like look. Known for its spirited personality, its confident bearing and its nimble movement.
Ancienne race sportive hongroise descend: An ancient Hungarian sporting breed descended from the hunting dogs of the Magyar tribes who settled in Hungary more than a thousand years ago. Developed by the Hungarian nobility as a versatile pointer and retriever, the breed survived the world wars thanks to devoted breeders.
Ancienne race suédoise remontant à plus: An ancient Swedish breed dating back more than 1,000 years to the Viking age, used as a versatile farm dog for driving cattle, controlling vermin and guarding. Also called the Västgötaspets, it probably shares ancestry with the Welsh Corgi.
Ancienne race toy de la Méditerranée au: An ancient Mediterranean toy breed with a long, silky white coat and a charming, playful personality, combined with a fearless temperament despite its small size.

Appelé autrefois chien picard, il était: Once called the chien picard, it was highly prized by the hunts with hounds of old France, in the days of Henri IV and Louis XIII. At the end of the 19th century, Le Couteulx de Canteleu still rated it one of the best breeds for hare, although it was already crossbred and hard to find pure; restoration attempts by Mr. Levoir and then Mr. Mallard fell short, and the breed was thought lost after World War II. In the early 1970s, Mr. Audréchy, of Buigny-lès-Gamaches in the Somme, rebuilt the stock with Mrs. Pilat. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 28), the Artois Hound remains very rare, with 57 dogs registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
Après la Première Guerre mondiale, des c: After World War I, German hunters including Rudolf Friess, Walter Zangenberg and Carl-Erich Grünewald left the Fox Terrier club to create a black and tan terrier bred solely for its hunting ability. Starting from black and tan terriers given to them by a zoo director, Lutz Heck, and from crosses with the old English wirehaired terrier and the Welsh Terrier, they set the type, and the German breed club was founded in 1926. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 103), the Jagdterrier is very widespread among French hunters, with nearly 600 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.

Au milieu du XIXe siècle, le comte Josep: In the mid-19th century, Count Joseph de Carayon-Latour, hoping to revive the declining Saintonge hound, crossed its last representatives with Baron de Ruble's Bleu de Gascogne hounds: the Grand Gascon Saintongeois was born, at the cost of the original Saintongeois disappearing. In the mid-20th century, huntsmen in southwest France selected the smallest dogs in their litters to establish the Petit Gascon Saintongeois, first intended for hare. The two varieties share a single FCI standard (no. 21), and the breed, well established among hunters, passed 600 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
Au XIXe siècle, plusieurs auteurs décriv: In the 19th century, several writers described black or black and white spaniels in Picardy, known as northern spaniels (épagneuls du Nord). In the early 20th century, the blue dogs were still shown alongside Picardy Spaniels before their identity was recognized; according to tradition, English Setter blood contributed to their coat color. The standard was registered in 1938, and the breed, recognized by the FCI (standard no. 106), shares its club with the Picardy Spaniel and the Pont-Audemer Spaniel. It remains rare in France, with 84 LOF registrations in 2025.
Aucun chien n’est fait pour rester seul: No dog is made to stay alone eight hours a day, every day. Some more independent breeds do cope better with your absences, though. Think about a dog walker or doggy daycare too.

Ce chien indigène de la Iakoutie (Républ: This native dog of Yakutia (the Sakha Republic), in northeastern Siberia, has accompanied the peoples of the Far North for centuries, pulling sleds, hunting and guarding reindeer herds. The first written mentions date back to the 17th century, and a first standard was drawn up in 1958. Threatened in the 20th century by the mechanization of transport and by crossbreeding, the breed was revived by Russian breeders, then given a standard in 2005 by the Russian Cynological Federation (RKF). The FCI provisionally recognized it in 2019 (no. 365); in France, its success has been rapid, with 481 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.

Cette fiche réunit trois des cinq taille: This profile covers three of the five German Spitz sizes: the large (about 45 cm), the medium (35 cm) and the small (27 cm). The toy size (Pomeranian) and the wolf size (Keeshond) have their own profiles. All share the fox-like head, the full ruff and the plumed tail curled over the back. Lively, attentive and very attached to its owner, the German Spitz is wary of strangers and has no prey drive at all, which makes it an easy family dog and a watchful guardian, quite fond of barking.
Cette race n’est pas reconnue par la Féd: This breed is not recognized by the Fédération Cynologique Internationale: no puppy can be registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF), and it is very rare in France. The information below comes from the clubs abroad that follow it.
Cette variété se rencontrait surtout dan: This variety was found mainly in the Pyrenean foothills, where livestock dealers and cattle drovers valued it highly. Its distinctive traits earned it an appendix to the Pyrenean Sheepdog standard as early as the 1920s, in the days of Bernard Sénac-Lagrange. Today the FCI recognizes it as a breed in its own right (standard no. 138), and it is looked after by the same breed club as the long-haired variety. Much rarer than the latter, it has about 75 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) a year.
Chaque race est notée de 1 à 5 sur 20 cr: Each breed is rated from 1 to 5 on 20 criteria: energy, children, cats, apartment living, time alone, barking, training, shedding, heat… The ratings come from FCI standards, breed clubs and veterinary sources, reviewed breed by breed in October 2026, then harmonized so they can be compared. The percentage shows how well a breed matches your criteria. The breed photos are generated by artificial intelligence, all in the same studio style, so the breeds can be compared like for like. A dog is still an individual: the breed gives a tendency, not a guarantee.
Chien ancestral de Picardie, façonné par: An age-old dog of Picardy, shaped by the region’s varied landscapes, from the plains to the marshes of the Somme, it long remained confined to its home province, which explains why it is not widespread. Set apart as a breed in the early 20th century, it shares its breed club with the Blue Picardy Spaniel and the Pont-Audemer Spaniel. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 108, revised in 2023), it is enjoying renewed interest among hunters, with 168 LOF registrations in 2025.
Chien ancien, puissant et robuste de typ: An ancient, powerful and sturdy Arctic spitz-type dog, known for its distinctive lion-like mane, its unique blue-black tongue, its stilted gait and its dense double coat.

Chien Chinois à Crête, petit chien de Ch: Chinese Crested, a small dog from China (23 to 33 cm, 2 to 5.5 kg). Moderate energy, fair with children. Temperament, health, care and 20 ratings.
Chien compact à queue courte, au visage: A compact, short-tailed dog with a distinctive flat face, upright ears and a smooth coat with “tuxedo” markings. Known as “the American Gentleman” for its friendly, intelligent temperament.
Chien compact de construction carrée, au: A compact, square-built dog with a long, abundant double coat and large, snowshoe-like feet suited to snow. Despite its name, it is not a terrier but a companion dog, nicknamed the “holy dog of Tibet”.
Chien courant ancien de taille moyenne c: An ancient, medium-sized hound known for the distinctive ridge of hair along its back, its muscular, athletic build and its independent, protective temperament.
Chien courant anglais utilisé pour chass: An English scent hound used to hunt hare in packs, documented since at least the 13th century. Older than the English Foxhound, it is thought to descend from old scent hounds such as the Talbot and from French hounds; Foxhound input later helped to establish it.
Chien courant athlétique de taille moyen: An athletic, medium-sized scent hound bred to hunt hare in packs, resembling a smaller English Foxhound, with a sturdy build, a short, dense coat and excellent stamina.
Chien courant athlétique, de taille moye: An athletic, medium to large hound with a distinctive tricolor coat, bred to track raccoons and drive them up trees. Fast, tireless and intelligent, it has a powerful, recognizable voice.
Chien courant athlétique, profilé et pui: An athletic, streamlined and powerful scent hound with a distinctive brindle coat, known for its intelligence, its courage and its exceptional tracking ability. Originally bred to hunt big game, including bear and wild boar.
Chien courant bas sur pattes, à l'ossatu: A low-slung, heavy-boned scent hound with characteristic long, velvety ears, a mournful expression and loose skin. Known for its powerful tracking ability and its calm temperament.
Chien courant compact et joyeux à la sil: A compact, cheerful scent hound with a sturdy build, a characteristic tricolor or bicolor coat and a merry temperament. Originally bred to hunt hare in packs, with a distinctive baying voice.
Chien courant de taille moyenne à grande: A medium to large, athletic scent hound with a striking solid red coat, known for its speed, its agility and its powerful tracking ability. Lean and muscular, this breed was developed specifically to hunt raccoons.
Chien courant de taille moyenne à la rob: A medium-sized scent hound with a fawn coat of very harsh, dry hair, the Griffon Fauve de Bretagne is a rugged, brave and resourceful hunter that handles hare and fox as well as roe deer and wild boar. Very gentle with people, sociable, affectionate and well balanced, it remains a hunting dog that needs wide open spaces and plenty of activity.
Chien courant de taille moyenne au poil: A medium-sized scent hound with a long, shaggy, coarse coat, always with a black overlay and ranging from wolf gray to fawn, the Griffon Nivernais has the rugged, tousled look that earned it the nickname “barbouillaud”. With a very keen nose, brave when holding game at bay without being reckless, it is above all a wild boar hunting specialist, in a pack or a small group, far more than a companion dog.
Chien courant de taille moyenne, à la tê: A medium-sized scent hound with a lean, noble head framed by very long ears, the Swiss Hound comes in four coat varieties: Bernese, Bruno du Jura, Lucerne and Schwyz. Lively and keen, it usually hunts alone, giving voice as it trails hare, roe deer or fox, while remaining gentle, docile and very attached to its owner.
Chien courant de taille moyenne, bien ch: A medium-sized scent hound, well built and balanced, with a tricolor or gray tricolor coat, the Beagle-Harrier takes after both the Beagle and the Harrier it descends from. A tireless hunter with a resonant voice, it hunts hare in a pack or a small group, but also roe deer, fox or wild boar; it is above all a hunting dog, and rarely kept as a companion.

A medium-sized scent hound, well built and fast, the Anglo-Français de Petite Vénerie has a short, close coat in tricolor, white and black, or white and orange. Keen, tireless and blessed with a fine voice, it hunts hare, rabbit, roe deer or fox, in a pack or in a small group. Sociable and easy to keep in a kennel, it remains a pack dog made for hunting, and is rarely kept as a companion.
Chien courant de taille moyenne, fin et: A medium-sized scent hound, refined and distinguished, the Porcelaine owes its name (French for “porcelain”) to its dazzling white coat, as glossy as glazed earthenware, dotted with rounded orange spots, especially on the ears. Gentle, sensitive and endearing with people, in the field it is a passionate specialist of hare and roe deer, with a fine nose and a melodious voice. It is first and foremost a hunting dog, and it copes poorly with inactivity and confinement.
Chien courant de taille moyenne, musclé: A medium-sized scent hound, muscular and heavy-boned, with a massive but not heavy head and a fawn-brown coat with a black mantle or saddle, the Bruno Saint-Hubert Français gives an impression of power and nobility. Lively, tenacious and brave, yet gentle and very attached to its owner, it hunts alone or in a pack on any terrain and is especially effective on wild boar and at blood tracking.
Chien courant du Sud-Ouest à la robe bla: A scent hound from southwest France with a white coat spotted with black and marked with pale tan, the Gascon Saintongeois comes in two varieties, the Grand and the Petit, which differ mainly in size. A pack hound with a keen nose and a beautiful voice, it hunts roe deer, wild boar and hare in a full pack or a small group. Calm and affectionate, it remains a hunting dog first and foremost rather than a companion dog.
Chien courant élégant et puissant, haut: An elegant, powerful scent hound, long-legged and light-boned, known for its remarkable stamina, its speed and its musical voice. One of the oldest American breeds, bred to hunt in packs over long distances.
Chien courant léger, élégant et distingu: A light, elegant and refined scent hound with a white coat clearly marked with black, the Ariégeois is a valuable helper on difficult ground, hunting alone or in a pack. A hare specialist that flushes its quarry with plenty of initiative, it also hunts roe deer and wild boar; cheerful and sociable, it takes direction easily for a scent hound.

German Wirehaired Pointer, a large dog from Germany (57 to 68 cm, 25 to 34 kg). Boundless energy, good with children. Temperament, health, care…
Chien d'arrêt de taille moyenne, compact: A medium-sized, compact and energetic pointing dog, white and orange, white and liver or white and black, with a fine, lightly feathered coat. Versatile at pointing as well as retrieving, this agile hunter combines stamina and intelligence.
Chien d'arrêt élégant et athlétique, rec: An elegant, athletic pointing dog, recognizable by its flecked (belton) coat, silky feathering and graceful gait. Passionate in the field, it is gentle and very sociable at home.
Chien d'arrêt élégant et musclé, à la ro: An elegant, muscular pointing dog with a flat, silky white and liver coat, feathered on the ears, legs and tail, the French Spaniel is one of the oldest pointing breeds in Europe. Steady, gentle, calm and docile, it holds a very firm point and retrieves willingly, and makes an ideal family companion as long as it can burn off energy every day.
Chien d'arrêt élégant et puissant, le Po: An elegant and powerful pointing dog, the English Pointer wins people over with its athletic outline, its short, close coat and its spectacular point, head high and tail straight out. A fast, tireless and wide-ranging hunter, it is renowned for the keenness of its nose. Gentle and affectionate at home, it remains a dog of wide open spaces that needs to run every day.
Chien d'arrêt hongrois de taille moyenne: A medium-sized Hungarian pointing dog with a dense, harsh coat in golden rust. Sturdy yet lean, and very versatile, it was bred to point and retrieve on rough terrain.
Chien d'arrêt polyvalent au poil dur et: A versatile pointing dog with a harsh, coarse coat and a pronounced beard and eyebrows. Known for its pointing, its retrieving and its way of hunting close to the hunter, it has an intelligent, cooperative character.
Chien d'arrêt robuste et charpenté, reco: A sturdy, solidly built pointing dog, recognizable by its harsh “wire” coat, its beard and its bushy eyebrows, the German Wirehaired Pointer was bred to do everything in the hunt, in open fields, woods and marshes, before and after the shot. Steady, well-balanced and very attached to its owner, it is more reserved with strangers and needs a demanding hunting or sporting life.

Chien d'Eau Espagnol, moyen chien d'Espa: Spanish Water Dog, a medium-sized dog from Spain (40 to 50 cm, 14 to 22 kg). High energy, fair with children. Temperament, health, care and 20 ratings.
Chien d'eau français de taille moyenne a: A medium-sized French water dog with a characteristic long, dense, curly coat and webbed feet, bred to retrieve waterfowl. Known for its rustic, athletic build and its cheerful, intelligent temperament.
Chien d'eau rustique de taille moyenne a: A hardy, medium-sized water dog with a distinctive curly, woolly coat, an athletic build and versatile working skills.
Chien d'eau rustique de taille moyenne,: A rugged, medium-sized water dog with a dense, curly, waterproof coat and an exceptional sense of smell. It is the only breed recognized as a truffle-hunting specialist.
Chien d'oysel allemand (Wachtelhund), mo: German Spaniel, a medium-sized dog from Germany (45 to 54 cm, 18 to 25 kg). Boundless energy, good with children. Temperament, health, care…

Chien de berger agile de taille moyenne: An agile, medium-sized herding dog with a striking multicolored coat, expressive eyes and keen herding instincts. Known for its intensity at work and its weather-resistant double coat.
Chien de berger athlétique de taille moy: An athletic, medium-sized herding dog with exceptional energy and intelligence, developed to work sheep over vast distances in tough Australian conditions. Known for its lithe, agile build and its tireless drive to work.
Chien de berger bas sur pattes, solide e: A low-set, sturdy and well-built herding dog with a fox-like head and a lively expression. Some are born with a short tail, others with a full tail, which the FCI standard accepts. Intelligent and hardy, it has an unmistakable look.
Chien de berger bas sur pattes, solideme: A low-set, solidly built herding dog with a long body, a bushy, fox-like tail and rounded ears, known for its intelligence and versatility.
Chien de berger de taille moyenne à la s: A medium-sized herding dog with an athletic, muscular build and a distinctive brindle coat. An intelligent, versatile and work-driven breed from the Netherlands, it once served as an all-around farm dog.
Chien de berger de taille moyenne au lon: A medium-sized herding dog with a long, shaggy double coat and a lively expression, known for its exuberant, charismatic personality and its characteristic bouncing gait.
Chien de berger de taille moyenne, athlé: A medium-sized herding dog, athletic and well proportioned, with a proud bearing, a short fawn coat with black overlay and a black mask. Highly intelligent and very eager to work, it is especially valued by police and armed forces.
Chien de berger de taille moyenne, très: A medium-sized herding dog, highly intelligent and athletic, with a keen expression and an intense working drive, famous for its instinctive ability to control livestock with its distinctive fixed stare.

A medium-sized herding dog, highly intelligent and versatile, with a dense double coat and a strong work ethic. An all-purpose farm dog, it is devoted to its family and adapts easily. This American breed is recognized by neither the FCI nor the Société Centrale Canine (French Kennel Club), so it is absent from the LOF. Not to be confused with the Old English Sheepdog.
Chien de berger élégant et athlétique de: An elegant, athletic, medium-sized herding dog with a long double coat ranging from rich fawn to mahogany with a black mask, known for its intelligence, versatility and strong drive to work.
Chien de berger et de chasse de taille m: An athletic, medium to large herding and hunting dog, known for its distinctive spotted or merle coat patterns, its striking odd-colored (heterochromatic) eyes and its great drive for work. This versatile dog excels at herding as well as hunting.
Chien de berger hongrois compact et de t: A compact, medium-sized Hungarian herding dog, known for its distinctive, naturally corded coat that looks like dreadlocks, giving it an agile, athletic outline with quick, spirited movement.
Chien de berger hongrois de taille moyen: A medium-sized Hungarian herding dog, agile and lively, with a mischievous terrier-like expression, a coat of corkscrew curls and upright ears with tipped-over points. Always on the alert, it is tireless at work.

Chien de berger kangal, géant chien de S: Kangal Shepherd Dog, a giant dog from Sivas (71 to 81 cm, 40 to 65 kg). Moderate energy, fair with children. Temperament, health, care and 20 ratings.
Chien de chasse de taille moyenne et com: A compact, medium-sized hunting dog with a distinctive red and white coat and straight, silky feathering. Known for its cheerful temperament, boundless energy and versatility in the field.
Chien de chasse de taille moyenne, énerg: A medium-sized, energetic and graceful hunting dog from Hungary, with an elegant golden rust coat and an athletic build. Known for its affectionate, gentle nature, it is a versatile hunter and an excellent family companion.
Chien de chasse de type spitz de taille: A medium-sized, fox-like spitz-type hunting dog with a dense, golden-red double coat, pricked ears and a plumed, curled tail. The national dog of Finland, it signals game perched in trees by barking, hence its nickname, the “barking dog”.
Chien de chasse élégant et athlétique co: An elegant, athletic gun dog known for its gorgeous, flowing mahogany or chestnut-red coat and its energetic, friendly temperament.
Chien de chasse polyvalent, athlétique e: A versatile, athletic and noble hunting dog with a short, dense coat in the typical liver and white, known for its intelligence, energy and friendly temperament.
Chien de chasse puissant et musclé au pe: A powerful, muscular hunting dog with a distinctive wavy, waterproof double coat and amber eyes, bred to retrieve waterfowl in the harsh conditions of Chesapeake Bay.
Chien de compagnie compact de type spitz: A compact spitz-type companion dog with a dense white double coat, black lips, nose and eye rims, a wedge-shaped head and a plumed tail carried over the back. It comes in three sizes (toy, miniature and standard) and stands out for its bright, alert expression.
Chien de compagnie compact et très muscl: A compact, very muscular companion dog with a broad head and a confident bearing, descended from the American Pit Bull Terrier and other bull-type breeds. It is known for being affectionate and attached to its family. In France, since it is not registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF), this dog is usually classed as Category 1 after a veterinary assessment of its build: acquiring, transferring or importing one is banned, sterilization is mandatory, and you need a dog ownership permit, a muzzle and a leash in public places.
Chien de Montagne des Pyrénées, géant ch: Great Pyrenees, a giant dog from the Pyrénées mountains (65 to 82 cm, 40 to 60 kg). Calm energy, good with children. Temperament, health, care…
Chien de protection des troupeaux majest: A majestic and very powerful livestock guardian dog with a thick white double coat and a natural guarding instinct shaped by work in the mountains.
Chien de protection des troupeaux massif: A massive, powerful livestock guardian dog with a thick, weatherproof double coat. Imposing and formidable, it was bred to defend flocks against wolves, bears and thieves in the Caucasus Mountains.
Chien de Saint-Hubert, grand chien de Be: Bloodhound, a large dog from Belgium (58 to 72 cm, 40 to 54 kg). Moderate energy, good with children. Temperament, health, care and 20 ratings.
Chien de taille moyenne, athlétique, au: A medium-sized, athletic dog with a distinctive white coat spotted with black or liver and an elegant outline, originally bred as a carriage dog with exceptional stamina.
Chien de traîneau athlétique sélectionné: An athletic sled dog selected for performance rather than looks, which is why coat colors and builds vary so much. It is not a recognized breed, by either the FCI or the Société Centrale Canine (French Kennel Club), but a type of working dog known for its exceptional speed and stamina.
Chien de traîneau de travail de taille m: A medium-sized, athletic working sled dog with a thick double coat, a striking wolf-like look and upright triangular ears, bred for endurance sledding in harsh Arctic conditions.
Chien de trait arctique de type spitz, d: An Arctic spitz-type draft dog of remarkable strength and sturdiness, the Alaskan Malamute is a large sled dog with a thick double coat, a deep chest and a well-muscled body. It has a wolf-like look and carries its plumed tail over its back.
Chien de travail compact et musclé, à la: A compact, muscular working dog with a distinctive blue or red speckled coat and exceptional stamina, bred to drive cattle. It is also called the “Heeler” because it moves livestock by nipping at their heels.
Chien de travail de taille moyenne, bien: A medium-sized, well-muscled working dog with an elegant, athletic outline and a smooth coat. Known for its lively, alert and self-assured temperament, it is one of the oldest German breeds.
Chien de travail de taille moyenne, puis: A medium-sized working dog, powerful and athletic, with a short muzzle and a short coat. Known for its playful, cheerful nature and expressive face, it combines boundless energy with great gentleness toward its family.
Chien de travail des bergers pyrénéens d: A working dog of Pyrenean shepherds for centuries, it remained almost unknown to the official dog world until the early 20th century, as its type varied a great deal from one valley to the next. During World War I, Pyrenean Sheepdogs served as messenger dogs and searched for the wounded. Its first standard was drawn up between 1921 and 1925 by Bernard Sénac-Lagrange, then revised several times by its breed club. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 141), it has about 350 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) a year and shines both with flocks and in agility.
Chien de travail géant et majestueux à l: A majestic giant working dog with a lion-like look, a thick, water-resistant double coat and a gentle, even temperament. This powerful yet serene breed combines an imposing presence with a natural calm.
Chien de travail massif et puissant conn: A massive, powerful working dog known for its outstanding water rescue skills and its gentle temperament. Often called “the gentle giant”, this breed has a thick, water-resistant double coat, webbed feet and a natural rescue instinct.
Chien de type primitif élégant et de tai: An elegant, medium-sized primitive-type dog with a short fawn coat and a lively expression, able to “blush” on its nose and ears when excited. Graceful, powerful and fast, it hunts by sight as much as by scent and hearing.
Chien de type primitif, élégant et léger: An elegant, light primitive-type dog from Central Africa, with a curled tail, a wrinkled forehead and a short, fine coat. Nicknamed the “barkless dog,” it expresses itself with yodel-like sounds rather than real barking.
Chien de type spitz de taille moyenne, a: A medium-sized spitz-type dog with balanced proportions and a thick, plush double coat that comes in a variety of colors. Known for its calm, devoted nature and self-assured temperament.
Chien de type spitz de taille moyenne, r: A sturdy, medium-sized spitz-type dog with a thick, abundant double coat and a gentle expression. Bred by the Sami people to herd reindeer, it handles Arctic cold with ease.
Chien de type spitz petit à moyen au pel: A small to medium spitz-type dog with an abundant, pure white double coat, a fox-like face with a pointed muzzle and a plumed tail carried over the back. This lively companion has an alert, friendly temperament.

Chien national de Malte, où on l'appelle: The national dog of Malta, where it is called “Kelb tal-Fenek” (rabbit dog) and traditionally hunts rabbits. Its name suggests Egyptian ancestors brought over by the Phoenicians, but genetic studies do not confirm this direct descent.
Chien nu du Mexique (Xoloitzcuintle), mo: Xoloitzcuintli, a medium-sized dog from Mexico (25 to 60 cm, 4.5 to 25 kg). Moderate energy, fair with children. Temperament, health, care and 20 ratings.
Chien près de terre, long de corps et tr: Low to the ground, long in the body and very muscular, the Dachshund is a passionate, lively and persistent hunter, with a remarkable nose and a strong personality. This profile covers the whole breed: three coat varieties (smooth, wire and long) and three sizes (standard, miniature and rabbit, or kaninchen), for nine recognized varieties. Originally an earth dog and a blood-tracking dog, it is now one of the most popular companions in France.
Chien puissant et athlétique à poil cour: A powerful, athletic, short-coated dog of molosser type, with a broad head and well-developed muscles, known for its confidence, strength and loyalty to its family. It was bred for farm work and guarding. In France, this dog is not registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF) and is not named in the 1999 law, but a veterinary assessment can place it in Category 1 based on its build: check before getting one.

Chien robuste de taille moyenne à la bar: A sturdy, medium-sized dog with the trademark beard and eyebrows, a square build and a wiry coat. An intelligent, spirited breed that works equally well as a versatile working dog and as a loyal companion.
Chien rustique de taille moyenne, sec et: A hardy, medium-sized dog, lean and muscular, with a short or medium-length coat that is most often brindle fawn, the Cursinu is the traditional dog of Corsica. Versatile, it works as a herding dog for livestock, a house guard and a wild boar flushing dog. Attached to its owner and wary of strangers, it needs space, activity and firm training.

Comme les autres variétés, il est issu d: Like the other varieties, it comes from the selection carried out from 1891 by Professor Adolphe Reul among Belgian herding dogs. It is named after the royal Château of Laeken, near Brussels, where shepherds used these dogs to guard the Crown's flocks; they were also used around Boom to watch over linen cloth laid out to bleach in the fields. Recognized within the single Belgian Shepherd Dog standard (FCI no. 15), the variety has become extremely rare: France registered only 4 with the LOF in 2025.
Comme tous les bassets, il est issu de c: Like all bassets, it comes from larger dogs, in this case the Grand Griffon Vendéen. The first selection work was done in the late 19th century by Count d'Elva, who was looking for straight-legged dogs, then Paul Dezamy set the type, keeping it tall enough to run down hare with a pack. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 33), it shares its breed club with the three other Vendéen breeds. It has earned a fine reputation abroad, especially in the United Kingdom, but remains rare in France, with about fifty registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) a year.

Connu en Allemagne depuis le Moyen Âge,: Known in Germany since the Middle Ages, the Dachshund descends from Bracke-type hounds and bassets bred to dig out badgers and foxes, hence its German name, Dachshund, or “badger dog”. The German Dachshund Club, the oldest club for the breed, was founded in 1888, and breeding was organized early on around three sizes and three coats. The FCI gives it a whole group, Group 4, of which it is the only breed. The current standard (2021) defines the three sizes by chest girth, not by height or weight. In France, it is among the breeds most often registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF), with 5,582 registrations in 2025, the wirehaired variety narrowly ahead of the smooth and the long-haired.
Considéré comme l'un des plus anciens ch: Considered one of the oldest French scent hounds, the Porcelaine is believed to descend from the Montaimbœuf and old Swiss hounds, and it survived in the border regions between Franche-Comté and Switzerland. It vanished from France during the Revolution and was rebuilt there in the 19th century from dogs kept in Switzerland, with packs recorded as early as 1845. Its FCI standard (no. 30) dates from 1964. It remains one of the French scent hounds most prized by hunters, with 384 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
Considéré comme l'une des plus anciennes: Considered one of the oldest British cattle dog breeds. According to tradition, its ancestors arrived in Wales with the Celts. Developed in Cardiganshire as a versatile farm dog, it drove cattle by nipping at their heels and guarded the farm.
Contemporain du Saint-Hubert, le Grand b: A contemporary of the Bloodhound, the Grand Bleu de Gascogne made up the 14th-century packs of Gaston Fébus, Count of Foix, who used it against wolves, bears and wild boar. Widespread in southern and southwest France, it is the ancestor of all the so-called “Midi” (southern French) hound breeds, and exported dogs contributed to American breeds such as the Bluetick Coonhound. Recognized by the FCI under no. 22, it is used today for gun hunting of big game and sometimes for hunting with hounds. In France, about a hundred puppies a year are registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF).

Déjà décrit en 1598 par le naturaliste i: Already described in 1598 by the Italian naturalist Aldrovandi, the Braque du Bourbonnais is a pointing dog from central France, known for its ruggedness. In the 1930s, breeders tried to impose a “faded lilac” color and a requirement to be born with a short tail, a selection so strict that it put the breed at risk. A team of breeders revived it from the 1970s onward, and the FCI recognizes it under no. 179. It remains rare, with around sixty registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) a year.

Des chiens de ce type apparaissent dans: Dogs of this type appear in paintings and prints as early as the 17th century, but the modern breed was fixed in the late 19th century in central Brittany, with some English Setter blood. The breed club and the first standard date from 1907.
Des chiens leveurs très semblables exist: Very similar flushing dogs have existed for centuries in German hunting with hounds, and the name “Wachtelhund”, quail dog, is an old one. Controlled breeding began in the early 20th century with a first registered dog, Lord Augusta, from Upper Bavaria, and a few females; Rudolf Friess then kept the brown and roan varieties apart to preserve the diversity of a narrow breeding base. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 104, flushing dogs group), it is valued by French hunters for driven hunts and blood tracking, with more than 450 dogs registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
Descendant des chiens d'oysel décrits pa: Descended from the chiens d’oysel (bird dogs) described by Gaston Phébus in the Middle Ages, it is considered the ancestor of many varieties of hunting spaniels. Its first standard was drawn up in 1891 by James de Connick, then revised several times. Threatened with extinction in the early 20th century, the breed was saved by Father Fournier, who gathered its best dogs, and its breed club was founded in 1921. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 175), it had 236 LOF registrations in 2025 and remains mostly a hunter’s dog.
Descendant des chiens de conduite romain: Descended from Roman droving dogs, developed in the German town of Rottweil as a cattle-driving and guard dog. Known as the “Rottweil butcher's dog,” it protected the butchers' money on their travels.
Descendant des chiens utilisés en Anglet: It descends from the dogs used in England for bull-baiting, which was banned in 1835. Fanciers then bred a calmer, stockier companion dog; the Bulldog Club, founded in 1875, wrote its first standard. An emblem of British tenacity, it is now the focus of breeding efforts to improve its breathing and health.
Descendant des épagneuls toy continentau: Descended from the continental toy spaniels prized at European courts for centuries, which appear in paintings by masters such as Titian, Goya and Rubens. The breed was refined in France and Belgium.
Descendant des épagneuls toy prisés par: Descended from the toy spaniels prized by European nobility since the 16th century, and famously associated with King Charles II. Its modern flat-faced look was developed through crosses with Asian breeds in the 19th century.
Descendant des Old English Bulldogs appo: Descended from Old English Bulldogs brought to the southern United States by working-class immigrants. Developed as an all-around farm utility dog for guarding property, catching livestock and protection. The breed was saved from extinction after World War II by breeders John D. Johnson and Alan Scott.
Descendant des spitz allemands blancs am: Descended from the white German Spitz dogs brought to the United States by German immigrants. During World War I, anti-German sentiment led to the breed being renamed “American Eskimo.” A circus star in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, it was recognized by the AKC in 1995, but not by the FCI.
Descendant du Old English Black and Tan: Descended from the Old English Black and Tan Terrier, it was bred as a ratter in Victorian England and is now a rare companion breed. Recognized by the Kennel Club (UK).
Descendant présumé du chien des tourbièr: Thought to descend from the Stone Age peat dog and the dogs of the lake dwellings, the German Spitz is considered the oldest breed in Central Europe and the source of many others. Long a guardian of farms, vineyards and boats, it became a popular companion dog in the 18th and 19th centuries, all the way to the royal courts of Europe. The FCI groups all its sizes in a single standard (no. 97), whose current version dates from 2024. In France, the Société Centrale Canine (French Kennel Club) does not separate the sizes: 2,666 German Spitz were registered in its LOF stud book in 2025, including 2,320 “other colors” (Pomeranians included) and 346 Keeshonds.
Descendant probable des Alans, et notamm: Probably descended from the Alaunts, and notably from the Alaunt vautre described by Gaston Phébus in the 14th century, the dogue was known almost only in Aquitaine by the mid-19th century, where it was used to hunt wild boar, guard homes and livestock, work for butchers and fight. It appeared under its current name at the first French dog show, at the Jardin d’acclimatation in Paris in 1863, and its first standard was published by Pierre Mégnin in 1896. Threatened with extinction after World War II, the breed revived in the 1960s, thanks in particular to Raymond Triquet, author of the 1971 standard, then gained worldwide fame with the film “Turner & Hooch” (1989). Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 116), the breed had 517 LOF registrations in 2025.
Développé à Bedlington, dans le Northumb: Developed in Bedlington, Northumberland, in the early 19th century to hunt vermin in mines and on farms. Poachers liked it, hence its nickname, the “gypsy dog.” Its ancestors are thought to include the Dandie Dinmont Terrier, the Whippet and the Otterhound.
Développé à Boston dans les années 1870: Developed in Boston in the 1870s by crossing the English Bulldog with the now-extinct White English Terrier. Refined in the late 19th century, it became one of the first breeds developed in the United States to be recognized by the AKC.
Développé à la cour de Weimar en Allemag: Developed at the court of Weimar in Germany in the early 19th century by German nobles who wanted a versatile hunting dog for big game. The breed's ancestry was a closely guarded secret.
Développé à la fin du XIXe siècle dans l: Developed in the late 19th century in the Malines (Mechelen) region of Belgium, it is one of the four varieties of the Belgian Shepherd. First bred to guard flocks, it was quickly adopted by law enforcement and armed forces around the world for its eagerness to work.
Développé à la fin du XIXe siècle par le: Developed in the late 19th century by the Dutchman Eduard Karel Korthals, who worked in Germany and France, by crossing various European pointing dogs and griffons. His goal: the ideal versatile pointing dog for hunting on foot. The FCI assigns it to France, where the breed mainly developed.
Développé à Munich à la fin du XIXe sièc: Developed in Munich in the late 19th century from the Bullenbeisser, an extinct big-game hunting dog, crossed with the English Bulldog. A guard dog, it was one of the first police and military dogs in Germany, before becoming a very popular family dog.
Développé à partir d'ancêtres de type Bi: Developed from Bichon-type ancestors brought over by Spanish settlers, it became the companion of the Cuban aristocracy. Nearly extinct after the Cuban Revolution, it was saved by Cuban families who fled to the United States.
Développé à partir de Bergers allemands: Developed from white-coated German Shepherds. When white was excluded from the German standard in the 1930s, breeding continued in North America, from where the dogs came back to Europe. Switzerland got the breed recognized: it was entered in the Swiss stud book in 1991, then recognized by the FCI in 2003 (definitively in 2011), hence its name.
Développé au début des années 1900 en Ca: Developed in the early 1900s in South Carolina by L. Whitaker Boykin. The foundation sire was a small stray spaniel-type dog named “Dumpy” who showed great hunting ability. The breed was created by crosses with the Chesapeake Bay Retriever, the Springer Spaniel and the Cocker Spaniel.
Développé au début du XXe siècle aux Éta: Developed in the early 20th century in the United States by crossing small Smooth Fox Terriers with toy breeds including the Chihuahua, the Manchester Terrier and the Italian Greyhound, to create a smaller, versatile companion.
Développé au début du XXe siècle par l'e: Developed in the early 20th century by polar explorer Arthur Treadwell Walden, who crossed mastiff-type dogs with Huskies and Belgian Shepherds. Named after its founding male, “Chinook”, it was bred to be a powerful sled dog with great stamina.
Développé au Japon dans les années 1920-: Developed in Japan in the 1920s and 1930s from various spitz breeds, including large white German Spitz brought to Japan around 1920. The breed was shaped through selection for its friendly temperament.
Développé au milieu du XIXe siècle en An: Developed in mid-19th-century England by gamekeepers, who crossed the English Mastiff with the English Bulldog to create an effective guard dog for tracking down poachers.
Développé au XIXe siècle dans la vallée: Developed in the 19th century in the Aire valley in Yorkshire by crossing the Otterhound with local terriers. Workers in the area used it to hunt otters and rats; its intelligence and courage later made it a police dog, a war dog and a versatile companion.
Développé au XIXe siècle dans le Staffor: Developed in the 19th century in Staffordshire, England. After bull-baiting was banned in 1835, bulldog and terrier crosses were used mostly for dog fighting and ratting. When these practices died out, breeders turned it into the affectionate, loyal companion it is today. The Kennel Club recognized it in 1935.
Développé au XIXe siècle dans les vallée: Developed in the 19th century in the Fox and Wolf river valleys of Wisconsin as a compact, versatile hunter able to work from a small boat. Its ancestors probably include the Irish Water Spaniel and the Curly-Coated Retriever. Wisconsin’s state dog since 1985, it contributed to the creation of the Boykin Spaniel. The AKC recognized it in 1940; the FCI does not recognize it.
Développé au XIXe siècle le long de la b: Developed in the 19th century along Chesapeake Bay from two shipwrecked Newfoundland-type puppies (Sailor and Canton) crossed with local retrievers, to create a hunting water dog able to withstand icy waters and strong currents.
Développé au XVIIIe siècle dans les coll: Developed in the 18th century in the Cheviot Hills along the English-Scottish border by farmers and shepherds to hunt foxes alongside packs of foxhounds. It had to be small enough to follow quarry into burrows and have enough stamina to keep up with the horses.
Développé au XVIIIe siècle, associé au D: Developed in the 18th century and linked to the French Duc de Noailles and to the Duke of Newcastle’s Clumber Park estate in Nottinghamshire. Probably descended from crosses between the Alpine Spaniel and the Basset Hound. Prized by the English nobility for hunting.
Développé aux États-Unis à partir de Coc: Developed in the United States from English Cocker Spaniels imported in the late 19th century. American breeders selected a smaller dog with a rounder head and a fuller coat, first for hunting quail and woodcock, then for the show ring. Recognized as a separate breed by the AKC in 1946, it belongs to FCI group 8.
Développé aux États-Unis à partir des ch: Developed in the United States from collie-type farm dogs brought over from England and Scotland by early settlers. It was used to drive livestock, guard the farm and hunt vermin. Only the United Kennel Club (UKC) recognizes it, and has done so since 1927.
Développé aux États-Unis au début du XXe: Developed in the United States in the early 20th century from European terriers brought over by British immigrants, including the Fox Terrier and the Manchester Terrier, for vermin control on farms and for companionship. President Theodore Roosevelt is said to have given the breed its name.
Développé aux États-Unis au XIXe siècle: Developed in the United States in the 19th century from bull and terrier type dogs brought over from England and Ireland. Its English ancestors fought bulls, but the American Pit Bull Terrier was mainly bred for dogfighting, before also serving as a farm dog and companion. The United Kennel Club recognized it in 1898; the FCI does not recognize it.
Développé aux États-Unis dans les années: Developed in the United States in the 1980s and 1990s as a companion dog, from the American Pit Bull Terrier, the American Staffordshire Terrier and other bulldog-type breeds, to produce a dog with a gentler temperament and a more massive build. Recognized by the United Kennel Club in 2013, it is not recognized by the FCI.
Développé aux Pays-Bas comme chien de fe: Developed in the Netherlands as an all-around farm dog for herding sheep and cattle, pulling carts and guarding. Nearly extinct after World War II, it was saved by dedicated breeding efforts.
Développé dans l'East Anglia en Angleter: Developed in East Anglia, England, in the 1880s as a sturdy earth terrier for ratting and bolting foxes. Officially separated from the Norfolk Terrier in 1964 on the basis of ear carriage (Norwich: prick ears, Norfolk: drop ears).
Développé dans l'ouest de l'Angleterre à: Developed in the west of England in the late 18th century, probably from old herding dogs such as the Bearded Collie and the South Russian Ovcharka. It drove cattle and sheep to market. According to tradition, its tail was docked to show it was a working dog exempt from tax, hence its name “bobtail” (short tail).
Développé dans la région de la rivière A: Developed in the Alapaha River region of southern Georgia as a versatile catch dog to control cattle and hogs and guard the farm. The Lane family preserved it in the 20th century from the old plantation bulldogs. Its full name, Alapaha Blue Blood Bulldog, refers to its bloodline (“blue blood”), not to its coat color. It is not recognized by the FCI.
Développé dans le canton de Berne, en Su: Developed in the canton of Bern, Switzerland, as an all-around farm dog for guarding, driving cattle and pulling carts, especially to deliver milk. Having become rare by the late 19th century, it was saved in the early 20th century by passionate Swiss breeders, including Professor Albert Heim.
Développé dans le Lancashire, en Anglete: Developed in Lancashire, England, as a versatile farm dog to drive cattle by nipping at their heels and to hunt rats. It is thought to come from crosses between the Welsh Corgi and the Manchester Terrier. The FCI has recognized it only provisionally, since 2016.
Développé dans le nord de l'Angleterre a: Developed in northern England in the 18th and 19th centuries by working-class families, who crossed small greyhounds with terriers for rabbit hunting and racing. The British Kennel Club recognized it in 1890.
Développé dans le nord de la Louisiane à: Developed in northern Louisiana from Native American dogs crossed with those of Spanish and French settlers, to hunt feral hogs and drive cattle. Named after Catahoula Parish, it is the official state dog of Louisiana.
Développé dans le Norfolk et l'East Angl: Developed in Norfolk and East Anglia, England, between the 1880s and the early 20th century as a farm dog to control vermin and hunt foxes. Originally classed as the drop-eared variety of the Norwich Terrier, it became a separate breed in 1964.
Développé dans le sud des États-Unis par: Developed in the southern United States by 18th-century settlers, from crosses between the English Foxhound, the Bloodhound and the Talbot, for raccoon hunting and trailing over the rugged terrain of the Appalachians.
Développé dans le sud des États-Unis, pr: Developed in the southern United States, mainly in Georgia, in the late 18th and early 19th centuries by Scottish immigrants. Created from red Irish Foxhounds and Bloodhounds to produce a fast, accurate tracking dog.
Développé dans les années 1840 par Heinr: Developed in the 1840s by Heinrich Essig in Leonberg, Germany, by crossing the Newfoundland, the Saint Bernard and the Great Pyrenees to create a “lion-like” dog recalling the lion on the town's coat of arms.
Développé dans les années 1970 à New Yor: Developed in the 1970s in New York by Tina Barber, who crossed large, old-style German Shepherds with Alaskan Malamutes and other breeds to create a bigger, calmer shepherd, with an emphasis on sound hips and a stable temperament.
Développé dans les Highlands écossais au: Developed in the Scottish Highlands in the mid to late 19th century by Dudley Marjoribanks (Lord Tweedmouth), who crossed a yellow retriever with the now-extinct Tweed Water Spaniel, with later additions of Irish Setter and Bloodhound blood.
Développé dans les Highlands écossais po: Developed in the Scottish Highlands to hunt fox, badger and vermin. The breeding of the white coat is credited to Colonel Edward Donald Malcolm of Poltalloch: legend has it that one of his reddish terriers was mistaken for a fox and killed by accident.
Développé dans les montagnes de Caroline: Developed in the mountains of North Carolina by German immigrant Johannes Georg Plott from German Hanoverian Schweisshunds brought over in the 1750s. Refined over generations to hunt big game in the Appalachians.
Développé dans les rudes îles Shetland e: Developed on the rugged Shetland Islands of Scotland as a small, hardy herding dog for sheep and ponies in harsh conditions. Created by crossing native dogs with Border Collies, Scotch Collies and possibly Spitz-type dogs.
Développé en 1899 par le capitaine Max v: Developed in 1899 by Captain Max von Stephanitz to create the ideal herding dog, standardized from local herding dogs. Its intelligence and ease of training led to its use by police and armed forces worldwide.
Développé en Afrique australe par croise: Developed in southern Africa by crossing the native ridged dogs of the Khoikhoi with European breeds such as Mastiffs and Greyhounds. Bred by farmers and hunters to track big game, especially lions, and hold it at bay.
Développé en Alaska par les mushers, qui: Developed in Alaska by mushers, who crossed northern dogs (Siberian Husky, Malamute, Inuit village dogs) with European breeds such as the Pointer, the Greyhound or the Saluki. The goal: to combine speed, stamina and the urge to run for sled racing, which it now dominates, in sprint and long-distance events alike.
Développé en Allemagne à la fin du XIXe: Developed in Germany in the late 19th century by crossing the Standard Schnauzer with smaller breeds such as the Affenpinscher and possibly the Poodle, to produce a more compact farm dog and ratter.
Développé en Allemagne au XIXe siècle à: Developed in Germany in the 19th century from the old German pointing dogs, themselves descended from Mediterranean pointers, with English Pointer crosses that refined the breed at the end of the century. The goal: a versatile pointing dog able to hunt in open fields, in woods and in water, and to retrieve.
Développé en Allemagne dans les années 1: Developed in Germany in the 1960s by Julius Wipfel, who crossed the Chow Chow, the Wolfspitz (Keeshond) and the Samoyed to create an ideal spitz-type companion dog. Recognized by the FCI.
Développé en Angleterre à la fin du XIXe: Developed in England in the late 19th century from the Cocker and other spaniels, first for the show ring, then bred back for work. Close to extinction after both world wars, the breed was rebuilt by a handful of breeders.
Développé en Angleterre au XIXe siècle e: Developed in 19th-century England by crossing bulldogs with terriers, at first for dog fighting. Around 1860, James Hinks established a more elegant white Bull Terrier; the famous egg-shaped head only became the norm in the early 20th century.
Développé en Angleterre aux XVIIIe-XIXe: Developed in England in the 18th and 19th centuries for fox hunting, its main job being to “bolt” foxes from their dens. Refined from various terrier and hound breeds, it was standardized by English fox hunters.

Developed in England in the 18th and 19th centuries for fox hunting, working above and below ground alongside packs of hounds to drive foxes out of their earths. One of the oldest recognized terrier breeds.
Développé en Angleterre comme chien de c: Developed in England as a versatile gun dog whose job was to find game and flush it (“to spring”), then retrieve it. Long told apart from the Cocker by size alone within the same litter, it was recognized as a separate breed by the British Kennel Club in 1902.
Développé en Angleterre il y a plus de 4: Developed in England more than 400 years ago from spaniel lines, then refined in the 19th century by Edward Laverack and R. Purcell Llewellin to create a gun dog specialized in finding and pointing game birds.
Développé en Argentine dans les années 1: Developed in Argentina in the 1920s by Dr. Antonio Nores Martinez, who systematically crossed the now-extinct Perro de Pelea Cordobés with the Great Dane, the Boxer, the Bull Terrier and the Pointer to create a versatile hunter.
Développé en Australie à la fin du XIXe: Developed in Australia in the late 19th century from working collies imported from Scotland, to produce a herding dog able to move sheep on its own over vast distances and in a harsh climate. The dingo ancestry often mentioned is a legend: genetic studies have not confirmed it.
Developed in Australia in the late 19th century by crossing Yorkshire Terriers with Australian Terriers to create a small companion dog with a long, silky coat, combining hardiness and refinement.
Développé en Australie au XIXe siècle à: Developed in Australia in the 19th century from British terrier breeds including the Cairn, the Skye and the Yorkshire Terrier. Bred as an all-round exterminator of rodents and snakes, and as a loyal watchdog.
Développé en Australie au XIXe siècle en: Developed in Australia in the 19th century by crossing British herding dogs, notably blue merle collies, with the dingo, then adding Dalmatian and black and tan Kelpie blood. The goal: a hardy cattle dog suited to the tough conditions of Australian ranching.
Développé en Bavière et dans le Wurtembe: Developed in Bavaria and Württemberg from the Standard Schnauzer, crossed with larger breeds such as the Great Dane or the Bouvier des Flandres. It drove cattle to market and guarded farms and breweries, before becoming a police dog in the early 20th century.
Développé en Californie à la fin des ann: Developed in California in the late 1960s from small Australian Shepherds, bred for a compact size while keeping its herding abilities. It became popular with riders competing in horse shows.
Développé en Écosse par Alexander, quatr: Developed in Scotland by Alexander, 4th Duke of Gordon, in the late 18th and early 19th centuries from black and tan setters. Established as a solid personal gun dog able to work long days over difficult Scottish terrain.
Développé en Flandre, en Belgique, comme: Developed in Flanders, Belgium, as a small guard dog and ratter, kept by craftsmen as well as on canal barges. Its name, often translated as “little boatman,” may also mean “little shepherd”: the FCI in fact classes it among the sheepdogs.
Développé en France au XIXe siècle lorsq: Developed in France in the 19th century, when English lacemakers brought Toy Bulldogs to France and crossed them with local ratters; it became very fashionable in Parisian society.
Développé en Hongrie aux XVIIe-XVIIIe si: Developed in Hungary in the 17th and 18th centuries by crossing the native Puli with German and French herding dogs and terriers. Used as a versatile farm dog to drive cattle, sheep and pigs.
Développé en Hongrie dans les années 193: Developed in Hungary in the 1930s by crossing the smooth-coated Vizsla with the German Wirehaired Pointer to create a hunting dog with a harsh, weatherproof coat, suited to rough terrain and harsh weather.
Développé en Irlande au XVIIIe siècle co: Developed in Ireland in the 18th century as a versatile gun dog for pointing and retrieving game birds, by crossing the Irish Water Spaniel, the English Setter and the Pointer. The breed's striking mahogany color became its hallmark.
Développé en Louisiane à partir de Grand: Developed in Louisiana from French Grand Bleu de Gascogne hounds crossed with English Foxhounds, American Foxhounds and other local coonhound breeds, and perfected for raccoon hunting on American terrain.
Développé en Nouvelle-Écosse, au Canada,: Developed in Nova Scotia, Canada, in the 19th century. It lured ducks by playing on the shore (“tolling”), then retrieved them once they had been shot. Recognized by the Canadian Kennel Club in 1945, then by the FCI.
Développé en Russie à partir de Toy Terr: Developed in Russia from English Toy Terriers in the early 20th century. It nearly died out after the Russian Revolution but was rebuilt from the surviving dogs after World War II, which led to the standardization of both varieties.
Développé par le peuple tchouktche de Si: Developed by the Chukchi people of Siberia as an endurance sled dog, able to pull light loads over long distances in the cold. Brought to Alaska in 1908 for sled racing, it became famous during the 1925 serum run to Nome. The breed was established in the United States, which the FCI recognizes as its country of origin.
Développé par les bergers de la frontièr: Developed by shepherds on the border between England and Scotland to herd sheep on the hills, and selected solely for its working ability. Most of today's Border Collies descend from one famous dog, Old Hemp, born in 1893.
Développé par les colons hollandais et e: Developed by Dutch and other European settlers in South Africa from the 1600s onward, from European mastiff breeds and local dogs. It was bred as an all-around farm dog to protect homesteads from predators such as leopards and baboons.
Développé par les moines de l'Hospice du: Developed by the monks of the Great St. Bernard Hospice, on the border between Switzerland and Italy, for rescue work in perilous Alpine conditions. Used to find and rescue travelers lost in the snow and fog.
Développé par les pêcheurs de l'île de T: Developed by fishermen on the island of Newfoundland for sea rescue, hauling nets and pulling carts. Descended from native water dogs and from European breeds brought over by fishermen.
Développé pendant la Révolution industri: Developed during the Industrial Revolution in Yorkshire and Lancashire by Scottish weavers and workers. Bred to catch rats in mills and mines by combining various terrier breeds, including the Clydesdale Terrier and the Skye Terrier.
Développé sur l'île de Skye en Écosse, l: Developed on the Isle of Skye in Scotland, it is one of the oldest terrier breeds. It was first used by Highland farmers to hunt foxes and vermin and drive them out of cairns (piles of stones), hence its name.

Grand chien courant américain puissant a: A large, powerful American scent hound with a distinctive black and tan coat and long ears, known for its exceptional nose, its loud bay and its determination on the trail.
Grand chien courant athlétique à la robe: An athletic large scent hound with a white and lemon or white and orange coat, the Great Anglo-French White and Orange Hound combines the keen nose of the Poitou hounds with the speed and stamina of the Foxhound. A pack hound above all, it hunts big game with great drive and a powerful voice. Sociable with other dogs and gentle with people, it lives in hunt kennels and is not suited to life as a companion dog.
Grand chien courant athlétique et musclé: A large, athletic and muscular scent hound with a distinctive blue-ticked coat and remarkable cold-trailing ability, bred specifically to track and tree raccoons.
Grand chien courant distingué à l'allure: A large, distinguished scent hound with a rustic look and a lemon-white or white and orange coat, the French White and Orange Hound is a pack hound bred for hunting with hounds (vénerie) and for big game. Calm and easy to live with in the kennel, like all pack-raised hounds, it is now the rarest of the French scent hounds and is nothing like a companion dog.
Grand chien courant du Poitou, bien bâti: A large scent hound from Poitou, well built, both strong and light, with a white or café-au-lait coat sometimes marked with pale orange or lemon, the Billy is a hound for mounted hunting, famed for its fine nose, its speed and its beautiful voice. A pack dog above all, trained to hunt roe deer and wild boar, it is keen and brave, and rarely lives as a mere companion dog.
Grand chien courant imposant, à l'expres: A large, imposing scent hound with a noble, dignified expression, recognizable by its wrinkled head, long drooping ears, loose skin and hanging jowls. Its extraordinary sense of smell makes it the most famous tracker of all dogs.
Grand chien courant majestueux, haut sur: A majestic large scent hound, tall on its legs, with a long head and very low-hanging ears, the Grand Bleu de Gascogne has a black and white ticked coat with a slate-blue sheen and tan markings above the eyes. Blessed with a very keen nose, it has a deep, howling voice that is famous among hunters. Calm and easy to handle, it is a pack hound meant for hunting big game rather than for life on the sofa.
Grand chien courant musclé et athlétique: A large, muscular and athletic scent hound with a distinctive ridge of hair along its back, originally bred to hunt lions in Africa. Known for its dignified, composed nature and its loyal temperament.
Grand chien courant puissant et bien cha: A powerful, well-built large scent hound with a short coat, usually tricolor with a black saddle, the Great Anglo-French Tricolour Hound combines the nose and voice of French hounds with the stamina and speed of the Foxhound. It is the most widespread breed in French hunting packs: a pure pack hound living in kennels, not suited to family life.
Grand chien courant puissant et endurant: A powerful, tireless large scent hound, the Great Anglo-French White and Black Hound has a white coat with a large black saddle or broad black patches, and pale tan markings above the eyes and on the cheeks. It excels at hunting red deer and roe deer with hounds in dense or wet country. Friendly, close to people and easy to manage in kennels, it lives in a pack with French hunts and is almost never a companion dog.
Grand chien courant très distingué, qui: A large and very distinguished scent hound that combines strength, elegance and lightness, with a short, glossy coat that is tricolor with a black saddle or large patches, the Poitevin is one of the jewels of French hunting with hounds. Fast, tireless and gifted with an exceptional nose, it is a true pack hound, kept in kennels by the hunts that ride to hounds, and almost never a companion dog.
Grand chien d'arrêt élancé et athlétique: A large, sleek and athletic pointing dog with a distinctive silver-gray coat and striking amber or blue-gray eyes. Fast, tireless and intelligent, it was first bred to hunt big game; its coat and stealth earned it the nickname “gray ghost”.
Grand chien d'arrêt italien, noble et pu: A large Italian pointing dog, noble and powerful, with a chiseled head, long drooping ears and a white coat, plain or marked with orange or brown. From an old Italian line, it is known for its keen nose and its steady point.
Grand chien d'ordre distingué et équilib: A large, distinguished and well-balanced pack hound (chien d’ordre), with a short coat that must be white and black, often ticked with black or blue, the French White and Black Hound is a keen-nosed, diligent and serious hunter with a fine voice. Highly valued by roe deer hunts, friendly and close to people, it lives in a pack in kennels and is not meant to be a companion dog.
Grand chien d'ordre élégant et bien musc: An elegant, well-muscled large pack hound with a tricolor coat and bright, sometimes coppery tan markings, the French Tricolour Hound is a pack dog created for grande vénerie, the French tradition of hunting big game with hounds: red deer, roe deer and wild boar. Brave, tireless and blessed with a very keen nose, it lives in a hunt pack alongside other hounds. It is not a companion dog, and neither apartment life nor being left home alone suits it.
Grand chien de berger athlétique et puis: A large, athletic and powerful herding dog with a long, shaggy double coat in its typical gray and white, famous for the hair that falls like a curtain over its face and for its distinctive bear-like gait.
Grand chien de berger puissant à l'appar: A large, powerful herding dog with a rugged look and a harsh, tousled double coat. This compact breed gives an impression of great strength without heaviness, with a dense, weatherproof coat.
Grand chien de chasse athlétique au pela: A large, athletic gun dog with a distinctive glossy black and tan coat. Sturdily built for work on rough ground, it is the heaviest and most imposing of the setters, known for its stamina and loyalty.
Grand chien de chasse robuste et musclé: A large, sturdy and muscular gun dog with a distinctive hard, dense coat, an expressive beard and eyebrows, and a patient, gentle expression. Built for hunting over any terrain, with a rustic yet versatile frame.
Grand chien de garde de troupeaux hongro: A large, muscular Hungarian livestock guardian dog with a distinctive heavy coat of white cords that looks like a mop. Built for endurance and protection, this imposing breed has a dignified, brave temperament.
Grand chien de garde de troupeaux puissa: A large, powerful, heavy-boned livestock guardian dog with a distinctive fawn coat, a black mask and ears and a curled tail, bred to protect flocks from predators.
Grand chien de protection des troupeaux: A large livestock guardian dog from Turkey, with an all-white coat and an athletic, lean build. Independent and very protective, it lives among the livestock; its color helped shepherds tell it apart from wolves at a distance.
Grand chien de traîneau américain athlét: A large, athletic American sled dog with a distinctive tawny double coat, known for combining strength, stamina and a calm, gentle temperament. This versatile working breed was developed for draft work and hauling.
Grand chien de travail athlétique aux or: A large, athletic working dog with erect ears, a noble expression and a confident bearing. Known for its great intelligence, loyalty, courage and versatility in herding and working roles.
Grand chien de travail élancé, athlétiqu: A large, sleek, athletic and powerful working dog with a proud, watchful bearing. Known for its exceptional loyalty and intelligence, it combines strength, elegance and agility.
Grand chien de travail fort et robuste a: A large, strong and sturdy working dog with a distinctive long tricolor coat and a calm, gentle temperament. One of the four types of Swiss mountain dog, it is known for its kind nature, its loyalty and its qualities as an exceptional family companion.
Grand chien de travail puissant et robus: A large, powerful and sturdy working dog with a hard, dense, weatherproof coat, the trademark beard and eyebrows, and an imposing presence. Originally bred for driving cattle and guarding.
Grand chien de travail robuste et musclé: A large, sturdy and muscular working dog with a black coat and tan markings, known for its strength, its protective instinct and its self-assurance. A loyal guardian, it is deeply attached to its family. In France, it is a Category 2 restricted dog, whether or not it is registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF): dog ownership permit, behavioral assessment, liability insurance, and a muzzle and leash in public places.
Grand chien de type molosse puissant à l: A large, powerful molosser-type dog with a sturdy build, a calm, attentive expression and the imposing presence of a self-assured guardian.
Grand chien puissant de type spitz origi: A large, powerful spitz-type dog from Japan, with a dense double coat, small erect ears and a tail curled over its back. Finer in the head than the American Akita, it impresses with its dignity and its brave, loyal temperament.
Grand et puissant chien de berger frança: A large, powerful French herding dog with a luxurious long, wavy double coat, a distinctive beard and eyebrows that fall like a curtain over the face, and a loyal, intelligent temperament.

A large, powerful French herding dog with characteristic double dewclaws, a short double coat and black and tan markings. Known for its confident bearing and its versatility as a guardian and companion.
Grand et puissant chien de garde de trou: A large, powerful Hungarian livestock guardian dog with a dense white double coat, a noble bearing and a fiercely loyal, protective temperament.
Grand et puissant chien de type molosse: A large, powerful, all-white molosser-type dog with a massive head and an athletic build, originally developed to hunt big game with exceptional courage and strength.

A large, powerful Italian molosser with a muscular, athletic build and a self-assured temperament. Historically used as a guardian and hunter, this intelligent, majestic breed is known for its loyalty and courage.

Grande race de berger bien équilibrée dé: A large, well-balanced shepherd breed developed from the German Shepherd, with a plush double coat, bred specifically for a calmer, gentler temperament and better health than the traditional German Shepherd.
Grande variété du Braque français, le ty: The large variety of the Braque Français, the Gascogne type is a powerful, sturdy pointing dog with strong limbs, supple skin, long ears and a brown or brown and white coat, often speckled. Calm, gentle and close to its owner, it hunts methodically and adapts to any terrain. Easy to live with, it suits a hunting family with plenty of space.
