Il descend des chiens courants réunis à: It descends from the scent hounds brought together at the end of the 17th century by the Marquis François de Larye, in Haut-Poitou, to hunt wolves. Nearly wiped out by the Revolution and then by a rabies epidemic in the 19th century, the breed was rebuilt with English Foxhound blood. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 24), it now hunts mainly roe deer and wild boar with packs of hounds. Because its dogs are raised in packs, they are rarely registered one by one with the French Kennel Club (LOF), hence very irregular figures (110 in 2024, just one in 2025).
Il descend du Griffon fauve de Bretagne,: It descends from the Griffon Fauve de Bretagne, an old Breton scent hound whose coat and abilities it kept. Very popular in its home region in the 19th century, it gained national fame in the last thirty years of the 20th century, thanks to its many wins in the Coupe de France rabbit hunting trials. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 36), it hunts rabbit, hare, fox, roe deer and even wild boar, alone or in a small pack. Today it is one of the French scent hounds with the most LOF registrations (690 in 2025), and it has also won many fans abroad, especially in the United Kingdom.
Il descendrait des chiens ségusiens des: It is said to descend from the Segusian hounds of the Gauls and from the gray hounds of Saint Louis (King Louis IX), highly prized in the royal packs until Francis I came to prefer the white hounds. Kept by a few noblemen of the Nivernais, the breed seemed extinct by the time of the French Revolution, then was recreated a century later from dogs that had stayed in its home region, with input from the Vendéen, the Foxhound and the Otterhound. Its club was founded in 1925 and the breed is recognized by the FCI (standard no. 17). With 571 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025, it is one of the scent hounds most used by wild boar hunters in France.
Il doit son nom au révérend John « Jack: It owes its name to the Reverend John “Jack” Russell, a Devon parson and keen hunter, who in the 19th century bred a strain of fox terriers able to keep up with the foxhounds and then bolt the fox from its earth. Two breeds come from this strain: the Parson Russell Terrier, taller and squarer, and the Jack Russell Terrier, shorter in the leg, whose type was established in Australia, the breed's country of development according to the FCI. Provisionally recognized by the FCI in 2000, then definitively in 2003 (standard no. 345), it has become very popular in France, with 1,641 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
Il est créé à la fin du XIXe siècle par: It was created in the late 19th century by Gaston Hublot du Rivault, at the Château de Billy in Poitou, from the last white hounds of old French stock: Montemboeuf, Céris and Larrye. Almost wiped out by World War II, the breed was saved by his son, Anthony Hublot du Rivault, from a few surviving dogs. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 25), the Billy remains very rare and lives mostly in a few hunting packs: 12 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
Il est déconseillé avec de jeunes enfant: It is not advised with young children. Never leave a young child alone with a dog, whatever its breed.
Il est fixé dans les années 1950 par des: It was established in the 1950s by huntsmen who wanted a more French type of pack hound, less marked by English blood than the Anglo-French hounds, starting from tricolor Anglo-French hounds refreshed with Poitevin and Billy blood. Its standard became official in the 1960s, and the breed is recognized by the FCI (standard no. 219, revised in 2023). Well represented in French hunting packs, it almost never appears in individual registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF): 115 in 2024, none in 2025.
Il est issu du chien de Saintonge, dont: It descends from the Saintonge hound, whose origin remains uncertain but which probably owes much to the white “greffier” hounds of the 16th century. The current type appeared in the second half of the 19th century and was later refreshed with Poitevin and Gascon Saintongeois blood. Given a standard in 1957, revised in 2007 by the Club du chien d’ordre, it is recognized by the FCI (standard no. 220). Its population, estimated at about two thousand dogs in the late 2000s, lives almost entirely in hunting packs, which explains why individual LOF registrations are almost nonexistent (one in 2024, none in 2025).
Il est né au XIXe siècle de croisements: It was born in the 19th century from crosses between French hounds, notably the Poitevin and the Gascon Saintongeois, and the English Foxhound, at a time when hunts were trying to rebuild fast, tough packs. Long known by the generic term Anglo-French, these dogs were later split into separate breeds by size and coat color, the tricolor being recognized by the FCI under standard no. 322. It hunts red deer, roe deer, wild boar or fox with hounds in many hunts. Like other pack hounds, it is rarely registered individually with the French Kennel Club (LOF): 65 in 2024, none in 2025.
Il partage ses origines avec l'Akita jap: It shares its origins with the Japanese Akita, which descends from the Matagi bear-hunting dogs of the Akita region, crossed from 1868 onward with Tosas and Mastiffs for fighting. After World War II, American servicemen brought heavier Akitas of the Dewa line back to the United States, and American breeders developed them separately, since no pedigrees were exchanged with Japan. The FCI separated it from the Japanese Akita under the name Great Japanese Dog, then as the American Akita since 2006 (no. 344), keeping Japan as its country of origin. In France, about 550 puppies a year are registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF).
Il présente de nombreuses similitudes av: It has much in common with the old Bruno du Jura of the Saint-Hubert type, the heaviest form of the Swiss hounds, a type now abandoned in Switzerland. French breeders, brought together in the Club français des Brunos et des chiens courants suisses, carried on their own breeding program, suited to the needs of today's hunters. The Société Centrale Canine (French Kennel Club) recognized it in 2003 as a French breed (SCC standard no. 905, group 6), but the FCI has not recognized it so far. Its numbers remain modest, with 159 dogs registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.

Issu de Foxhounds anglais importés dans: Descended from English Foxhounds brought to colonial America as early as 1650, then adapted to American terrain and fox hunting. George Washington played a key role in its development by selecting lighter, taller and faster dogs able to hunt the red fox over varied terrain.
Issu des anciens épagneuls britanniques,: Descended from the old British spaniels, the Cocker owes its name to the woodcock, which it flushed for hunters. Long told apart from the Springer by size alone, it was recognized as a separate breed by the British Kennel Club in 1892; a dog named Obo, born in 1879, is considered the father of the modern breed. Dogs exported to America later gave rise to the American Cocker Spaniel.
Issu des bassets français, eux-mêmes des: Descended from the French bassets, themselves descendants of the hounds of the Abbey of Saint-Hubert, and bred to hunt rabbit and hare in thick cover. Imported to England in the second half of the 19th century, it was crossed there with the Bloodhound and fixed in its current type; this is why the FCI lists Great Britain as its country of origin.
Issu des chiens de type bull and terrier: Descended from bull and terrier type dogs that came from England to the United States in the 19th century, where they were used in dogfighting. Later bred to be heavier than the English Staffordshire Bull Terrier and used as a farm dog and companion, it was recognized by the AKC in 1936 as the Staffordshire Terrier, renamed American Staffordshire Terrier in 1972.
Issu des Foxhounds anglais importés en V: Descended from English Foxhounds brought to Virginia in 1742 by Thomas Walker. In the 19th century, Kentucky breeders, notably the Walker and Maupin families, added the blood of a fast dog of unknown origin, “Tennessee Lead”, to gain speed and scenting ability. It is not recognized by the FCI.
Issu des petits chiens de type barbichon: Descended from the small barbichon-type dogs of the Mediterranean, it was once called the Tenerife. A prized companion at European courts during the Renaissance, it was established as a breed in France and Belgium, where its standard was set in 1933 under the name Bichon à poil frisé.
Issu du Berger allemand à robe blanche,: Descended from the white-coated German Shepherd, the White Swiss Shepherd Dog is a large, athletic working dog with erect ears, a white double coat and a confident bearing. It stands out for its noble expression and gentle temperament.
Issu du Bull Terrier, dont il partage l': It comes from the Bull Terrier and shares its history: small dogs already existed in the breed in the 19th century. Bred for fans of a more compact companion, the miniature variety was recognized by the British Kennel Club in 1939.
Issu du chien de Saint-Jean, utilisé par: It descends from the St. John's dog, used by Newfoundland fishermen to retrieve nets and fish that slipped away. It was developed and established in England in the 19th century by the British aristocracy for waterfowl hunting, which is why the FCI assigns it to Great Britain.
Issu du Grand bleu de Gascogne, chien co: Descended from the Grand Bleu de Gascogne, a scent hound of medieval Gascony, and bred to hunt hare and small game. After becoming very rare, it was revived in the early 20th century by the breeder Alain Bourbon.

Les Petits bassets griffons vendéens ont: For a long time, Petits Bassets Griffons Vendéens shared the standard of the Grand Basset, differing only in size, which produced dogs too heavy for their work. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 67), the PBGV has become popular abroad, even winning Best in Show at Westminster in 2023, while it remains low-key in France, with 127 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.

On reconnaît déjà sa silhouette dans des: Its outline can already be recognized in 13th-century sculptures in Amiens Cathedral, then in 15th-century tapestries. A favorite of the ladies of the Burgundian court, it often appears in 17th-century painting, and Buffon described it in the 18th century, already noting its rarity. Having become extremely rare by the mid-20th century, it was saved by a handful of European breeders, and the French breed club was founded in 1947. Classed by the FCI among the bichons and related breeds (standard no. 233), it remains very little known in France, with 17 registrations with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
Originaire d'Allemagne, où de petits pin: Originally from Germany, where small wire-haired pinschers were already hunting rats in houses, kitchens and stables in the 17th century. The breed was established in Munich and Berlin. Its name means “monkey pinscher” (Affe is German for monkey): it is not a terrier, and the FCI classes it with the pinschers and schnauzers.
Originaire de l'Ariège, il est issu du c: Originally from Ariège, it comes from crossing the local briquet hounds with a large pack hound, the Bleu de Gascogne or the Gascon Saintongeois, keeping that type in a smaller, lighter frame. Its standard was set in the early 20th century, and the breed is recognized by the FCI (standard no. 20). It remains a hunters' dog, with just over 200 LOF registrations in 2025.
Originaire de la région de Pont-Audemer,: From the Pont-Audemer area, in the Eure department, it is thought to have arisen in the 19th century from crosses between old local spaniels and water dogs, probably the Irish Water Spaniel, from which it kept its curly coat. Decimated by the wars, the breed was narrowly saved in the second half of the 20th century by a controlled infusion of Irish Water Spaniel blood, under the guidance of the club it shares with the Picardy Spaniel and the Blue Picardy Spaniel. Recognized by the FCI (standard no. 114), it has only a few registered births each year in France (8 LOF registrations in 2025, 19 in 2024).
Originaire de la vallée de Glen of Imaal: Native to the Glen of Imaal valley in County Wicklow, it served as a versatile farm dog for hunting badger, fox and vermin, and once turned the spit in kitchens. Recognized by the Irish Kennel Club in 1934.
Originaire de Madagascar, où il était le: Native to Madagascar, where it was the companion of the nobility, it descends from small white bichon-type dogs that arrived with sailors and merchants. It is named after the port of Tuléar (Toliara) and was recognized by the FCI in 1987.
Originellement élevé par la noblesse all: Originally bred by the German nobility from mastiff-type dogs to hunt wild boar and deer, then refined as an estate guardian and companion. Declared the national dog of Germany in 1876.

Petit chien courant trapu et vigoureux,: A small, stocky and vigorous scent hound with a very harsh, dry coat in fawn shades ranging from golden wheaten to brick red, the Basset Fauve de Bretagne is a brave, resourceful and tenacious hunter. Petit chien de berger de type spitz puis: A small, powerful spitz-type herding dog with short legs, pointed ears, a curled tail and wolf-like markings. This ancient, fearless breed is often called “the Viking dog”.
Petit chien de berger robuste aux pattes: A small, sturdy herding dog with short legs and a low-set build. It has a short, weather-resistant black and tan double coat, a fox-like expression and an alert temperament.
Petit chien de berger sec et nerveux, au: A small, lean and wiry herding dog with a long or medium-length coat whose texture is somewhere between goat hair and wool, the Pyrenean Sheepdog packs remarkable energy into a small frame. Petit chien de compagnie robuste et enjo: A sturdy, cheerful little companion dog with a soft, curly white double coat, dark eyes and a lively, playful temperament.
Petit chien de type épagneul agile d'ori: A small, agile spaniel-type dog of Dutch origin with a distinctive orange-red and white coat, feathering and fringed ears, originally bred to lure ducks into traps.

A small, sturdy working terrier with a shaggy, weather-resistant coat and an alert expression, from the Scottish Highlands and known for its brave, cheerful temperament.
Petit terrier de travail robuste, agile: A small, sturdy, agile working terrier full of personality, with a supple body slightly longer than it is tall and a mostly white coat, the Jack Russell Terrier is lively, bold and fearless. An excellent companion for active owners, it needs plenty of exercise, things to do and consistent training to channel its energy and prey drive. Its coat can be smooth, rough or “wiry”.
Petit terrier musclé et compact, à la tê: A small, muscular and compact terrier with an egg-shaped head and small triangular eyes. A scaled-down Bull Terrier, it is known for its comical, mischievous and lively character and its square, sturdy build.
Petit terrier noir et feu élégant à l'os: A small, elegant black and tan terrier with fine bones and the trademark pointed, upright ears shaped like a candle flame.
Petit terrier noir et feu, compact et mu: A small, compact and muscular black and tan terrier, the German Hunting Terrier was created purely for work: digging out foxes and badgers, finding and flushing wild boar on driven hunts, tracking and retrieving. Brave, tenacious and tireless, it is no lapdog and suits only experienced owners, ideally hunters.
Petit terrier robuste au double pelage r: A small, sturdy terrier with a harsh double coat and a distinctive topknot, known for its keen, alert expression and its courageous personality.

Very intelligent, playful and easy to train, it makes a remarkable family companion, gentle with children and sensitive to the mood at home. Originally a waterfowl hunting dog, it still has a real need for physical and mental activity.
Plus petit chien de race du monde, le Ch: The smallest dog breed in the world, the Chihuahua has an apple-shaped head, large upright ears and a compact body that weighs no more than 3 kg. The companion dog par excellence, it comes in two varieties, short-haired and long-haired, covered by a single standard.
Plus petite variété du Caniche (24 à 28: The smallest Poodle variety (24 to 28 cm at the withers according to the FCI standard), with a dense, curly coat that barely sheds and a lively, attentive temperament. Plus petite variété du Spitz allemand, i: The smallest variety of the German Spitz, it descends from larger spitz dogs that were bred down in size in the Pomerania region. Présent en Corse depuis au moins le XVIe: Present in Corsica since at least the 16th century, the Cursinu was long the indispensable helper of the island’s shepherds, pig farmers and hunters, before declining in the second half of the 20th century in the face of imported breeds. The Association de sauvegarde du chien corse (Corsican Dog Preservation Association), founded in 1989, located and selected the last dogs true to type. The Société Centrale Canine recognized it in 2003 and places it in group 5 (spitz and primitive types); the breed is not recognized by the FCI. Today it has about 150 LOF registrations a year (153 in 2025).

Race ancienne chinoise connue pour ses r: An ancient Chinese breed known for its distinctive deep wrinkles, its hippopotamus-like muzzle, its blue-black tongue and its compact, medium-sized build, with a calm and independent temperament.
Race ancienne chinoise des provinces du: An ancient Chinese breed from the southern provinces, dating back to the Han dynasty, originally used as a versatile farm dog for hunting, guarding, herding and farm work. Nearly extinct by the mid-20th century, it was saved by an international rescue program.
Race ancienne d'Afrique centrale, souven: An ancient breed from Central Africa, often compared with the dogs shown in the art of ancient Egypt. The peoples of the Congo Basin, notably Pygmy peoples, used it as a versatile hunter for its speed and silence. It became established in England, then in the United States, in the 1930s.
Race ancienne d'Irlande utilisée à l'ori: An ancient breed from Ireland, originally used in war and to hunt wolves and the great Irish deer. It had nearly died out by the 1860s but was revived by Captain George Augustus Graham, who standardized the breed.
Race ancienne d'origine asiatique, arriv: An ancient breed of Asian origin that arrived in Hungary with the Magyar tribes in the 9th century (some authors point instead to the Cumans, in the 13th century). Bred as an independent livestock guardian, it protected sheep and cattle against wolves and bears.
Race ancienne de l'ouest de la Turquie,: An ancient breed from western Turkey, used for centuries to guard flocks. Its name means “white head” in Turkish (ak baş). Brought to North America in the 1970s to protect livestock from predators, it is not recognized by the FCI, so it cannot be registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF).
Race ancienne de la cour impériale chino: An ancient breed of the Chinese imperial court, revered in the Imperial Palace in Peking, where only the emperor's family could own one. It reached Europe in 1860, brought back by British troops after the sack of the Summer Palace.
Race ancienne de la région de Romagne en: An ancient breed from the Romagna region of Italy, originally used as a water retriever in the marshes. When the marshes were drained, the breed was adapted and became the world's leading truffle dog.
Race ancienne de lévrier développée dans: An ancient sighthound breed developed in the Scottish Highlands to hunt wild red deer. Once so prized that only the nobility could own one, it nearly died out with the decline of the clan system but was saved by devoted enthusiasts.
Race ancienne de lévrier développée par: An ancient sighthound breed developed by the nomadic Tuareg peoples of the Sahel region for hunting gazelle and other game, protecting livestock and keeping company. Bred for speed and endurance in Saharan conditions.
Race ancienne des montagnes du Caucase,: An ancient breed from the Caucasus Mountains, selected by shepherds for its courage, size and stamina. Standardized in the Soviet Union in the 20th century, it also served as a guard dog in the army and in prisons.
Race ancienne développée au Moyen Âge pa: An ancient breed developed in the Middle Ages by the monks of the Abbey of Saint-Hubert, in the Belgian Ardennes. Brought to England, where it took the name Bloodhound, it was valued for centuries for tracking game, then people, to the point of becoming indispensable to law enforcement.
Race ancienne développée dans les monast: An ancient breed developed in Tibetan monasteries and palaces more than a thousand years ago as an indoor sentinel dog, alerting the monks to intruders. Highly prized and rarely allowed to leave the country until it was introduced to England in the 20th century.

An ancient breed developed in Tibetan monasteries and refined by imperial breeders at the Chinese court. Probably descended from Tibetan breeds, possibly from crosses between the Lhasa Apso and the Pekingese, it was prized as a companion of the nobility.
Race ancienne développée il y a plus de: An ancient breed developed more than 2,000 years ago in the Buddhist monasteries of Tibet as a cherished companion, watchdog and herder. Known as “Holy Dogs” and “luck bringers”, they were never sold, only given as gifts.
Race ancienne développée par le peuple n: An ancient breed developed more than 3,000 years ago by the nomadic Samoyed people of Siberia to herd reindeer, pull sleds and keep them company. Their thick coat protected them from the brutal climate.
Race ancienne dont l'origine remonterait: An ancient breed whose origins are thought to go back more than 2,000 years in the Mediterranean basin. Prized by the nobility of ancient Greece, of Rome and later of Renaissance Italy, it was the companion of many European courts.
Race ancienne dont les racines sont attr: An old breed whose roots are traced to Dalmatia, in Croatia. It was first used as a carriage dog, able to run long distances alongside horse-drawn coaches and to guard the horses and carriages. It also had a career in circuses and became the emblem of American firehouses.
Race ancienne et primitive native de l'e: An ancient, primitive breed native to eastern Thailand, developed for hunting small game, controlling vermin and guarding. Its isolation in the region preserved its unique traits over the centuries.
Race ancienne native des îles Canaries,: An old breed native to the Canary Islands, originally developed as a versatile farm and guard dog to protect livestock and property, and used to catch and hold cattle. Nearly extinct in the 1960s, it was revived by dedicated breeders.
Race ancienne originaire de Chine, prisé: An ancient breed from China, prized by Chinese emperors and European nobility. Brought to Europe by Dutch merchants in the 16th century, it became the official dog of the House of Orange in the Netherlands.
Race ancienne prisée dans les monastères: An ancient breed prized in Tibetan monasteries for more than 2,000 years, developed by Buddhist monks as a companion and as a watchdog on the monastery walls. Often given as a precious gift to royalty and dignitaries.
Race ancienne probablement descendue de: An ancient breed probably descended from African or Mexican hairless dogs and refined in China. Chinese sailors kept them on ships to hunt vermin and traded them in ports around the world.
Race ancienne probablement originaire de: An ancient breed probably from the Chinese imperial court, later refined in Japan by the nobility as a lapdog and cherished companion. Often given as a gift to diplomats and royalty.
Race ancienne remontant à plus de 3 000: An ancient breed going back more than 3,000 years, with archaeological evidence of its presence in Mexico. Highly prized by the Aztecs, the Maya and other ancient cultures as a companion, healer, guardian and ceremonial animal.
Race ancienne utilisée depuis des siècle: An ancient breed used for centuries by shepherds in the Pyrenees to protect flocks from wolves and bears. Ses origines sont très anciennes : une m: Its origins are very old: a Roman mosaic found in Avenches already shows pack hounds close to today's varieties, and the Swiss Hound was sought after by the Italians from the 15th century, then by the French in the 18th century, for the demanding hunt of hare. Ses origines sont très anciennes et sans: Its origins are very old and probably shared with the wire-haired sheepdogs of northwestern Europe. The first Picards were judged at a dog show in 1863 alongside Beaucerons and Briards; Paul Mégnin wrote a first standard in 1922 and the breed was recognized in 1925. Still rare, the breed is clearly growing in France, rising from 136 to 240 registrations in the LOF stud book between 2024 and 2025.

Son élevage débute à la fin du XIXe sièc: Breeding began in late 19th-century Germany, in the wake of the Wirehaired Pointing Griffon (Korthals), then took shape in the early 20th century around the ideas of Baron von Zedlitz und Neukirch, known as “Hegewald”, who wanted a German wire-haired hunting dog that was effective and firm in character. Crosses between griffons, Stichelhaars, Pudelpointers and shorthaired pointers fixed the type, on the principle that working ability shapes the body. The German club (Verein Deutsch-Drahthaar) was founded in 1902, and the breed, recognized by the FCI (standard no. 98), is now one of the most widespread pointing dogs in Germany. In France, it appeals mostly to big-game hunters and fans of versatile dogs, with about 700 dogs registered with the French Kennel Club (LOF) in 2025.
